name: Company search count (base)
description: Count how many companies a search would match before paying for rows. Free: 0 credits. Takes the same filters, query or es_query as companies/search-base and returns a rounded total with no records, so a list can be sized and priced first (10 credits per row on the search card, which a team outside the price rollout pays, and 10 for teams in the price rollout). A filter on a field that identifies one company, such as a name, domain, LinkedIn URL or legion_id, is refused: use enrichment for that.

options.name: filters
options.about: Preferred input. An object keyed by the company record's own field names, for example {"industry": "software development", "size": ["51-200", "201-500"], "locations.country_code": "US"}. Every field given must hold. A value matches it, a list matches any of its values, {"gte": 2015} or {"lte": 2020} is a range, and {"exists": true} tests that the field is filled. Common fields: name.cleaned, domain, industry (a lowercase LinkedIn industry name), size (1-10, 11-50, 51-200, 201-500, 501-1000, 1001-5000, 5001-10000, 10001+), type (private, public, nonprofit, government_agency, educational), founded, tickers.symbol, and offices under locations.* (locations.city, locations.state_code, locations.country_code; add "locations.primary": true for the headquarters). Headcount, growth and other premium fields are refused on this base product. keywords takes a Boolean string over name, headline and description: "machine learning" OR robotics NOT consulting. Combine sets with {"and": [...]}, {"or": [...]} or {"not": {...}}, up to 3 levels. Case never matters. Send exactly one of filters, query or es_query.

options.name: query
options.about: SQL alternative to filters, for what filters cannot express: a SELECT * FROM companies WHERE ... statement Data Legion runs. Do not put LIMIT or OFFSET in it. Exchange does not execute this statement.

options.name: es_query
options.about: Elasticsearch-style alternative for code that builds queries, on the same field names as filters: {"bool": {"filter": [{"term": {"company_size": "51-200"}}, {"match": {"job_title": "product manager"}}], "must_not": [{"term": {"company_name": "acme"}}]}}. Supported types: bool (must, should, filter, must_not, minimum_should_match), term, terms, match, match_phrase, range, exists, prefix, wildcard and nested. Anything else is refused, including scripts, aggregations, regexp, fuzzy, query_string, sort and size. A filters search returns its compiled form as generated_query, which es_query accepts as is.

response.about: total is rounded: to the nearest 10 under 100, else to two significant figures. total_status says how to read it: about (the rounded count), at_least (a lower bound, the search was too broad to finish counting) or under (fewer than 10 match, possibly none). A filters count also returns generated_query. The warnings field, when present, holds Data Legion's note on how the search was read.

fields.name: total_status
fields.about: about, at_least or under.

fields.name: warnings
fields.about: Present only when Data Legion sent a note on how the search was read.

billing.description: 10 Firecrawl credits per returned person outside the price rollout, the same as the 0.01 enrichment card. Teams in the price rollout pay 5 per returned person instead. Your team's price is 5 credits where this says 10; other amounts scale by the same ratio.

A name alone is not a lookalike seed. Say only who to find, not how to search.

options.name: limit
options.about: Rows to return. Default 1. This product stops at 25 so the quote stays within 125 credits. The vendor's own maximum is 100.

options.name: cursor

options.name: offset
options.about: Rows to skip. 0 to 10000. Each call with an offset reads the query again, so pages can overlap or skip records.

options.name: titlecase
options.about: When true, Data Legion title-cases display text. Identifiers, URLs, and codes stay as stored.

options.name: include_fields
options.about: Comma-separated fields to keep. Omitted means the whole record.

name: Person search (base-no-contact)
description: Find people in the base-no-contact dataset by field filters such as job title, employer, industry and skills, to build a list when no single person is named. Send filters, an object of field names and values (preferred), a SQL SELECT in query, or an Elasticsearch-style es_query. To size a list first at no cost, use people/count-base-no-contact. The API key selects the dataset and field set, and a filter on a field outside it is refused. Each returned row is 10 credits on the card, the same as one successful base-no-contact enrichment, and 5 for teams in the price rollout. An empty page costs nothing. total is not billed. At most 25 rows, so the call stays within 125 credits.

billing.description: 10 Firecrawl credits per returned person outside the price rollout, the same as the 0.01 enrichment card. Teams in the price rollout pay 5 per returned person instead. Empty matches cost 0. The page stops at 25 so a call at the rollout price stays within 125 credits. Your team's price is 5 credits where this says 10; other amounts scale by the same ratio.

options.name: filters
options.about: Preferred input. An object keyed by the person record's own field names, for example {"job_title": ["vp of sales", "head of sales"], "company_industry": "software development"}. Every field given must hold. A value matches it, a list matches any of its values, {"gte": 5} or {"lte": 10} is a range, and {"exists": true} tests that the field is filled. Common fields: job_title (words in order, so "vp of sales" also finds "senior vp of sales"), company_name, company_domain, company_industry (a lowercase LinkedIn industry name), company_size (1-10, 11-50, 51-200, 201-500, 501-1000, 1001-5000, 5001-10000, 10001+), skills.cleaned, and work history under experience.* (experience.organization.name.cleaned, experience.title.cleaned, experience.current; given together they must hold for the same job). seniority_level, job_function, is_decision_maker and other premium fields are refused on this base product. Location, age and sex are contact data and are refused on this no-contact product: use a with-contact search to filter by place. keywords takes a Boolean string over title, headline, summary and skills: ("data engineer" OR "analytics engineer") AND python NOT intern. Combine sets with {"and": [...]}, {"or": [...]} or {"not": {...}}, up to 3 levels. Case never matters. Send exactly one of filters, query or es_query.

options.name: query
options.about: SQL alternative to filters, for what filters cannot express: a SELECT * FROM people WHERE ... statement Data Legion runs. Do not put LIMIT or OFFSET in it. Exchange does not execute this statement.

options.name: es_query
options.about: Elasticsearch-style alternative for code that builds queries, on the same field names as filters: {"bool": {"filter": [{"term": {"company_size": "51-200"}}, {"match": {"job_title": "product manager"}}], "must_not": [{"term": {"company_name": "acme"}}]}}. Supported types: bool (must, should, filter, must_not, minimum_should_match), term, terms, match, match_phrase, range, exists, prefix, wildcard and nested. Anything else is refused, including scripts, aggregations, regexp, fuzzy, query_string, sort and size. A filters search returns its compiled form as generated_query, which es_query accepts as is.

options.name: limit
options.about: Rows to return, in place of a LIMIT clause. Default 1. This product stops at 25 so the quote stays within 125 credits. The vendor's own maximum is 100.

options.name: offset
options.about: Rows to skip. 0 to 10000. Ordering can change between Data Legion builds.

options.name: cursor
options.about: next_cursor from the previous page, sent with the same filters, query or es_query and without offset. Reads past offset 10000. A cursor from another search or an older data build is refused.

options.name: titlecase
options.about: When true, Data Legion title-cases display text. Identifiers, URLs, and codes stay as stored.

options.name: include_fields
options.about: Comma-separated fields to keep. Omitted means the whole record.

options.name: exclude_fields
options.about: Comma-separated fields to drop after include_fields.

options.name: pretty_print
options.about: When true, Data Legion indents the JSON body.

response.about: One page of person records. next_cursor, when not null, is the cursor option for the next page. A filters search also returns generated_query, the query object the filters compiled to. total is not the number billed. Data Legion may send Total-Count-Status to say whether total is exact, an estimate, or this page. Exchange does not return that header, so treat total as possibly approximate. The warnings field, when present, holds Data Legion's note on how the search was read: a filter no stored value can match (the page is then empty and free), or an abbreviation or short pattern it searched differently.

name: Earnings calendar
description: Find who reports earnings when, or one company's reported and upcoming earnings with actual EPS, consensus estimate, and surprise. Pass symbols with from and to for a company's history; without symbols the window covers the whole market and to may be at most 31 days after from. A successful call costs 10 Firecrawl credits, including an empty list. Use fundamentals/company for full earnings history and trend.

billing.description: EODHD Enterprise is $2,499/month and every paid plan starts at 100,000 API calls a day, so one call costs at most about $0.00083. Fundamentals is 10 calls, about $0.0083; the other routes are 1. Any positive charge under $0.01 is 10 Firecrawl credits, so a successful call is 10. An HTTP error is free. The cap is 100.

options.name: from
options.about: Report-date window start, YYYY-MM-DD. Default today.

options.name: to
options.about: Report-date window end, YYYY-MM-DD. Default from plus 7 days. Without symbols, to is at most 31 days after from and needs from.

options.name: symbols
options.about: Up to 10 tickers, comma-separated without spaces, such as AAPL.US,MSFT.US. Narrows the date window, so set from and to as well.

response.about: Records in earnings, one per company and fiscal period. type and description label the response; from and to, or symbols, echo the request. actual is null before the report. difference is 0, not null, when estimate is missing. An empty list is still billed. A 404 means an unknown symbol and costs nothing.

fields.name: date
fields.about: Fiscal period end.

name: IPO calendar

options.name: to

response.about: Records in ipos, not sorted. A deal can appear more than once as it moves from Filed or Expected to Priced. price_from, price_to, offer_price, and shares are 0 when not known yet. An empty list is still billed.

name: Company fundamentals
description: Read company fundamentals for one listed stock, ETF, fund, or index on any of EODHD's 70+ exchanges, not only SEC filers: profile, highlights, valuation, share stats, holders, earnings history and trend, and yearly or quarterly balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow. Pass filter to keep the response small. A successful call costs 10 Firecrawl credits. Use symbols/search first when only a name is known, and prices/eod for price history.

options.name: filter
options.about: One section or field, nested with ::, several comma-separated. Examples: General, Highlights, Valuation, Financials::Balance_Sheet::yearly, General::Code. A single missing field answers the string NA. The cost is 10 API calls either way.

response.about: One object keyed by section. Stocks carry General, Highlights, Valuation, SharesStats, Technicals, SplitsDividends, Holders, InsiderTransactions, outstandingShares, Earnings, and Financials. ETFs, funds, and indices carry their own sections, such as ETF_Data or Components. With filter, only the named sections, or a bare value for one field. A 404 costs nothing.

name: Qcew list
description: To collect a county, state, MSA or national employment and wage table (area slice), one industry across every area (industry slice), or size-class detail (size slice, Q1), or to fetch the code books for joins. Hyphenated NAICS (31-33) may be given with the hyphen or the URL underscore.

options.about: Opaque `next_cursor` from the previous page (`<offset>@<etag>`). Pass the same year/qtr/slice/code (or titles) with it. A cursor whose slice has since been re-published fails with invalid_input, issue code publication_changed: restart without a cursor.

options.name: include_titles
options.about: Join area/industry/ownership/agglevel/size titles onto every row (default true; false saves two upstream fetches).

options.name: limit

response.about: QCEW Open Data rows (records/list): one whole CSV slice per call, `/cew/data/api/{year}/{qtr}/{area|industry|size}/{code}.csv` (area slice: every ownership x industry x aggregation level for one area; industry slice: every area for one industry; size slice: Q1 only, private ownership by establishment size class), paged from memory with `limit` rows per page. The cursor pins the slice's ETag: a page whose slice was re-published since (BLS revises prior quarters) fails with `invalid_input` at `/cursor` and issue code `publication_changed` instead of mixing versions. Codes stay strings; `disclosure_code` N rows carry null employment and wage measures (never 0) while the establishment count stays. Titles from area_titles.csv and industry_titles.csv (fetched) and the ownership, aggregation-level and size code books (embedded) are joined unless `include_titles` is false. `titles` alone lists a code book instead (area 9,459 rows, industry 2,678).

fields.name: commodity_subgroup_name

fields.name: commodity_group_name

fields.about: `FutOnly` or `Combined`, naming which report the row came from.
fields.name: futonly_or_combined

name: Disaggregated report, futures only
description: Physical commodities - agriculture, energy, metals - when the question is which kind of participant is positioned, not just speculator versus hedger: managed money is the fund positioning most reports quote, swap dealers carry the index-fund flow, producers and merchants are the physical hedge. Financial futures are not here; use the financial report.

options.about: CFTC contract market code, `088691` for COMEX gold. The stable id for a market across weeks and report types - names get edited, codes do not. Exact match.
options.name: cftc_contract_market_code

options.about: Market and exchange as the report prints them, `GOLD - COMMODITY EXCHANGE INC.`. Exact match, upper case; use `$where` with `upper()` or `like` for anything looser.
options.name: market_and_exchange_names

options.about: Commodity name, `GOLD` or `CRUDE OIL`. Exact match, upper case. One commodity can span several markets.
options.name: commodity_name

options.about: Exchange code: `CBT`, `CME`, `NYME`, `CMX`, `ICUS`, `ICEU`. Exact match, and unreliable on its own: a quarter of the rows store the code with trailing spaces (`CMX ` beside `CMX`, the latest gold row among them), and equality on `CMX` misses every one of those. Filter on `cftc_contract_market_code` instead, or use `$where=cftc_market_code like 'CMX%'`.
options.name: cftc_market_code

options.about: Top-level commodity group: `AGRICULTURE`, `FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS` or `NATURAL RESOURCES`.
options.name: commodity_group_name

options.about: One report date, as `2026-08-25` or the full `2026-08-25T00:00:00.000`. Reports are as of Tuesday and published Friday. For a range use `$where`.
options.name: report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd

options.about: Report week label, `2026 Report Week 34`. Exact match.
options.name: yyyy_report_week_ww

options.about: A SoQL filter for anything the column filters cannot say: `report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd > '2026-01-01' AND commodity_name = 'GOLD'`, `open_interest_all > 100000`, `market_and_exchange_names like '%CRUDE%'`. An unknown column answers HTTP 400 with the failing query echoed back.
options.name: $where

options.about: Sort, as `column ASC|DESC`, comma-separated for several. Defaults to `report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd DESC` for ordinary row queries. With `$select`, no default order is added; supply an order compatible with the selected columns.
options.name: $order

options.about: Rows to return. The default is 1,000; the datasets hold hundreds of thousands, so a date or market filter is what keeps a page useful rather than this.
options.name: $limit

options.about: Rows to skip, for paging past `$limit`.
options.name: $offset

options.about: Columns to return, comma-separated, in place of all of them. `count(*)` on its own answers how many rows match. A selected subset no longer matches the declared fields, so read the declared list as what the full row carries.
options.name: $select

response.about: A bare array, one row per market and report date. Every value is a JSON string, numbers included - Socrata serialises numeric columns as decimal strings - and a column whose value is null is left out of the row rather than sent as null. An empty array means nothing matched; a filter on an unknown column answers HTTP 400 rather than an empty array. Positions for producers/merchants/processors/users, swap dealers, managed money and other reportables, each long and short (and spreading for the last three), plus total reportable and non-reportable, for all, old and other crop months; then the weekly change, the percentage of open interest, the trader counts and the concentration ratios.

response.about: A bare array, one row per market and report date. Every value is a JSON string, numbers included - Socrata serialises numeric columns as decimal strings - and a column whose value is null is left out of the row rather than sent as null. An empty array means nothing matched; a filter on an unknown column answers HTTP 400 rather than an empty array. The same columns as legacy/futures-only, with options positions folded in on a futures-equivalent (delta-adjusted) basis. `futonly_or_combined` reads `Combined`.

name: Supplemental report, commodity index traders
description: Thirteen agricultural markets - corn, wheat, soybeans, sugar, coffee, cocoa, cotton, cattle, hogs - when the question is how much of the length is passive index money rather than a directional view. Nowhere else in the COT is index-trader positioning stated on its own.

options.about: CFTC contract market code, `088691` for COMEX gold. The stable id for a market across weeks and report types - names get edited, codes do not. Exact match.
options.name: cftc_contract_market_code

options.about: Market and exchange as the report prints them, `GOLD - COMMODITY EXCHANGE INC.`. Exact match, upper case; use `$where` with `upper()` or `like` for anything looser.
options.name: market_and_exchange_names

options.about: Commodity name, `GOLD` or `CRUDE OIL`. Exact match, upper case. One commodity can span several markets.
options.name: commodity_name

options.about: Exchange code: `CBT`, `CME`, `NYME`, `CMX`, `ICUS`, `ICEU`. Exact match, and unreliable on its own: a quarter of the rows store the code with trailing spaces (`CMX ` beside `CMX`, the latest gold row among them), and equality on `CMX` misses every one of those. Filter on `cftc_contract_market_code` instead, or use `$where=cftc_market_code like 'CMX%'`.
options.name: cftc_market_code

options.about: Top-level commodity group: `AGRICULTURE`, `FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS` or `NATURAL RESOURCES`.
options.name: commodity_group_name

options.about: One report date, as `2026-08-25` or the full `2026-08-25T00:00:00.000`. Reports are as of Tuesday and published Friday. For a range use `$where`.
options.name: report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd

options.about: Report week label, `2026 Report Week 34`. Exact match.
options.name: yyyy_report_week_ww

options.about: A SoQL filter for anything the column filters cannot say: `report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd > '2026-01-01' AND commodity_name = 'GOLD'`, `open_interest_all > 100000`, `market_and_exchange_names like '%CRUDE%'`. An unknown column answers HTTP 400 with the failing query echoed back.
options.name: $where

options.about: Sort, as `column ASC|DESC`, comma-separated for several. Defaults to `report_date_as_yyyy_mm_dd DESC` for ordinary row queries. With `$select`, no default order is added; supply an order compatible with the selected columns.
options.name: $order

options.about: Rows to return. The default is 1,000; the datasets hold hundreds of thousands, so a date or market filter is what keeps a page useful rather than this.
options.name: $limit

options.about: Rows to skip, for paging past `$limit`.

options.about: Columns to return, comma-separated, in place of all of them. `count(*)` on its own answers how many rows match. A selected subset no longer matches the declared fields, so read the declared list as what the full row carries.
options.name: $select

response.about: A bare array, one row per market and report date. Every value is a JSON string, numbers included - Socrata serialises numeric columns as decimal strings - and a column whose value is null is left out of the row rather than sent as null. An empty array means nothing matched; a filter on an unknown column answers HTTP 400 rather than an empty array. The legacy categories with commodity index traders broken out (`cit_positions_long_all`, `cit_positions_short_all`). The `_NoCIT` restatement is partial and the column names say which figures carry it: the non-commercial and commercial groups are restated in full - positions, weekly changes, percent of open interest and trader counts - while total reportable gets only percent of open interest and trader counts (`Pct_OI_Tot_Rept_Long_All_NoCIT`, `Traders_Tot_Rept_Long_All_NoCIT`) and non-reportable only percent of open interest. The total reportable position amounts and their changes are not restated, so `tot_rept_positions_long_all` and `change_tot_rept_long_all` still include index traders, and the non-reportable positions and changes are served as in the legacy report. There is no non-reportable trader count in any COT report, so none is restated here. Column names here are mixed-case as served - `NComm_Postions_Long_All_NoCIT` - and are declared exactly as they arrive. Futures and options combined; there is no futures-only supplemental.

name: Payment limits
description: For "what does Medicare Part B pay for Keytruda this quarter", "what is the ASP payment limit for J9271", "which HCPCS code bills NDC 00006-3026-02 and how many billing units does it hold" or "what does Medicare pay per unit for Opdivo". The payment limit is Medicare's allowance per HCPCS billing unit, generally 106% of the manufacturer-reported average sales price (ASP), so it is the closest free proxy for a net price of a physician-administered drug. For one code across quarters, use asp-pricing/payment_limit_history; for IRA negotiated prices, negotiated-prices/search; for pharmacy acquisition cost, data-medicaid-gov prices/search (NADAC); for Medicare spending, data-cms-gov drug-spending/search.

options.name: drug
options.about: Brand or generic name, matched case-insensitively anywhere in the code's short description (`Inj pembrolizumab`) or in a crosswalk drug name (`Keytruda`): `keytruda`, `pembrolizumab`, `trastuzumab`. Biosimilars are listed under their brand names (`zarxio`), so the generic name finds only the reference product.

options.name: hcpcs
options.about: A HCPCS Level II code, a letter and four digits: `J9271`. CPT codes (five digits) are AMA copyright and not served.

options.name: include_ndcs
options.about: List each code's NDCs from the crosswalk. Defaults to true when `drug`, `hcpcs` or `ndc` is given, false otherwise; `ndc_count` is always given. With `ndc`, only the matching NDCs are listed.

options.name: limit
options.about: Most codes to return.

options.name: ndc
options.about: An NDC-11 as 11 digits (`00006302602`) or hyphenated 5-4-2 (`00006-3026-02`), a hyphenated 10-digit NDC (4-4-2, 5-3-2 or 5-4-1), or an NDC-9 product code (`00006-3026`). A bare 10-digit NDC is ambiguous and rejected. Matches the crosswalk's NDCs.

options.name: offset
options.about: Codes to skip; pass `next_offset` for the next page.

options.name: quarter
options.about: Quarter the payment limits apply to, `2026-Q4`; defaults to the newest CMS has posted. `quarters_available` lists every quarter CMS links (from 2021-Q1). Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[Qq][1-4]$.

response.about: Medicare Part B payment allowance limits for drugs, per HCPCS Level II code, from CMS's quarterly ASP pricing file, joined to the ASP NDC-HCPCS crosswalk. Filter by brand or generic name, HCPCS code or NDC, for the newest quarter or any quarter CMS links from 2021-Q1; no filter pages through every code. Each code has its short description, billing unit (dosage), payment limit in USD per billing unit, beneficiary coinsurance percentage, the vaccine and blood AWP-based limits where they apply, CMS's notes, and its NDCs with drug name, labeler, package size and billable units. CPT-coded rows (AMA copyright) are left out. No match is an empty result.

fields.name: blood_awp_percentage
fields.about: Percent of AWP that sets a blood product's limit, where it applies.

fields.name: blood_limit
fields.about: Blood product payment limit in USD per billing unit, where it applies.

fields.name: clotting_factor
fields.about: CMS flags the code as a clotting factor (paid with a furnishing fee).

fields.name: coinsurance_percentage
fields.about: Beneficiary coinsurance percentage (20 unless reduced by inflation rebates); null in files before 2023-Q2.

fields.name: dosage
fields.about: The billing unit the limit is per: `1 MG`, `10 MG`, `1 UNIT`.

fields.name: ndc_count
fields.about: NDCs the crosswalk lists for the code.

fields.name: ndcs
fields.about: The code's NDCs from the crosswalk; only those matching `ndc` when it is given; null when `include_ndcs` is false.

fields.name: notes
fields.about: CMS's notes, lines joined with `; `: `8% of reference add-on applied`, `AMP-based payment limit`.

fields.name: payment_limit
fields.about: Payment allowance limit in USD per billing unit; null where CMS writes N/A (with the reason in `notes`) or the code is only in the crosswalk.

fields.name: short_description
fields.about: HCPCS short descriptor as CMS writes it: `Inj pembrolizumab`.

fields.name: vaccine_awp_percentage
fields.about: Percent of AWP that sets a vaccine's limit, where it applies.

fields.name: vaccine_limit
fields.about: Vaccine payment limit in USD per billing unit, where it applies.

name: Search
description: For "what is Medicare's negotiated price for Eliquis in 2026 and 2027", "which drugs were selected for 2028", "does NDC 00169-4130-13 have a maximum fair price" or "which negotiated drugs were deselected". These are Medicare negotiated prices only: for what Medicare Part B pays per HCPCS code each quarter (ASP payment limits), use asp-pricing/payment_limits; for what pharmacies pay, use data-medicaid-gov prices/search (NADAC); for Medicare and Medicaid spending on a drug, use data-cms-gov drug-spending/search.

options.name: drug
options.about: Brand name or active ingredient, matched case-insensitively anywhere in the selected drug's name (which lists its brands) or active ingredient: `eliquis`, `Wegovy`, `semaglutide`, `insulin aspart`.

options.name: include_ndcs
options.about: List each NDC-11 with its per-unit prices. Defaults to true when `drug` or `ndc` is given, false otherwise, so a list of selected drugs stays compact; `ndc_count` is always given. With `ndc`, only the matching NDCs are listed.

options.name: ipay
options.about: Initial price applicability year, the first year a drug's negotiated price applies: 2026 (10 drugs), 2027 (15), 2028 (15, selected January 2026).

options.name: limit
options.about: Most drugs to return; `total_count` counts every match.

options.name: ndc
options.about: An NDC-11 as 11 digits (`00169413013`) or hyphenated 5-4-2 (`00169-4130-13`), a hyphenated 10-digit NDC (`0169-4130-13`, 4-4-2, 5-3-2 or 5-4-1), or an NDC-9 product code (`00169-4130`, `001694130`). A bare 10-digit NDC is ambiguous and rejected. Matches the NDC-11, CMS's cross-referenced NDC-11 or the NDC-9.

response.about: Medicare's negotiated prices (maximum fair prices, MFPs) for the drugs CMS selected under the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, filtered by brand name or active ingredient, NDC or initial price applicability year; no filter lists every selected drug. Each drug has its brand names, active ingredient, initial price applicability year, a status (price in effect, agreed, pending or ended), the MFP per 30-day equivalent supply for each period including inflation adjustments, Part B HCPCS codes, CMS's deselection determination and MFP explanation file, and its NDC-11s with the per-unit MFP of each period, update type and remarks. No match is an empty result.

fields.name: active_ingredient
fields.about: Active ingredient or active moiety as CMS writes it: `APIXABAN`, `METFORMIN; SITAGLIPTIN`.

fields.name: brand_names
fields.about: The brands in `selected_drug_name`, as CMS writes them.

fields.name: deselection
fields.about: CMS's deselection determination from the page's "Drugs with Deselection Determinations" table (for example after a generic or biosimilar launched); null when the table does not list the drug. NDC prices marked `Deselect` in the file also show in `ndcs`.

fields.name: hcpcs_codes
fields.about: HCPCS codes CMS lists for the drug's NDCs (Part B drugs such as Botox `J0585`); empty for Part D drugs.

fields.name: initial_price_applicability_year
fields.about: The first year the negotiated price applies (IPAY).

fields.name: mfp_explanation_url
fields.about: CMS's MFP explanation for the drug (a ZIP of a redacted PDF on how CMS reached the price); null until CMS publishes one.

fields.name: mfp_per_30_day_supply
fields.about: The single MFP per 30-day equivalent supply, in USD, one entry per price, oldest first: the negotiated price, then each annual inflation adjustment. Empty while the price is pending. Prices CMS end-dated before they took effect (deselected drugs) are left out.

fields.name: ndc_count
fields.about: NDC-11s CMS lists for the drug.

fields.name: ndcs
fields.about: The drug's NDC-11s with their prices; only those matching `ndc` when it is given; null when `include_ndcs` is false.

fields.name: selected_drug_name
fields.about: The selected drug as CMS names it, brands separated by `; `: `OZEMPIC; RYBELSUS; WEGOVY`.

fields.name: source_url
fields.about: CMS's Selected Drugs and Negotiated Prices page.

fields.name: status
fields.about: Derived from the file's MFP periods and today's date: `price_in_effect` (a period covers today), `price_agreed` (published, starts later), `price_pending` (selected, no MFP published yet), `price_ended` (every period has ended).

fields.name: status_label
fields.about: The status in words with its date, plus any deselection: `Negotiated price in effect since 2026-01-01; deselected, removal effective 2027-01-01`.

DECISION AND ORDER DENYING PETITIONER'S MOTION TO VACATE, SET ASIDE OR CORRECT SENTENCE PURSUANT TO 28 U.S.C. § 2255: Pierre-Louis's motion for relief pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 2255 is denied; no hearing is necessary. See Chang v. United States, 250 F.3d 79, 86 (2d Cir. 2001) (in claims of ineffective assistance, affirming district court's decision to forego a full testimonial hearing where the court "reasonably decided that the testimony of [the defendant] and his trial counsel would add little or nothing to the written submissions"). Furthermore, Pierre-Louis has not made a substantial showing of a denial of a federal right, so no certificate of appealability shall issue. See, e.g., Hamilton v. Superintendent, 2017 WL 1944114, at *6 (S.D.N.Y. 2017) (declining to issue a Certificate of Appealability "because Petitioner has failed to identify a claim that jurists ofreason would find debatable as to whether Petitioner was denied such a right) (citing Slack v. McDaniel, 529 U.S. 473,478 (2000)); Prousalis v. United States, 2018 WL 3471811, at *5 (DLC) (S.D.N.Y. 2018) (citing Hojjl.er v. Bezio, 726 F.3d 144, 154 (2d Cir. 2013); Tankleffv. Senkowski, 135 F.3d 235,241 (2d Cir. 1998); Rodriquez v. Scully, 905 F.2d 24, 24 (2d Cir. 1990)). The Court finds that any appeal by Pierre-Louis from its Order would not be taken in good faith, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(a)(3). Id. (citing Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438,445 (1962)). This constitutes the decision and order of the Court. (Signed by Judge Colleen McMahon on 4/21/2022) (kv) (Entered: 04/21/2022)

name: Utilization
description: Look up a clinician's reported Medicare procedure occurrences, not unique patients, quality or outcomes. Check displayed_on_profile before showing profile-facing results; CMS does not give a reason for an N flag. Use the separate NPI Registry program for clinician identity.

The cursor pins the version uuid and the publisher's CSV SHA-1; every page re-reads both and fails with invalid_input at /continuation (issue code `publication_changed`) when the release moved, instead of mixing releases. name: Search
description: Questions about one drug or a few: "how much did Medicare spend on Eliquis in 2024", "how has Ozempic's cost per dose changed", "what does Medicaid pay for semaglutide", "what does Part B spend on Keytruda (J9271)". Use `top` for the biggest or fastest-growing drugs, and the `records_list` collector only to copy every row of a whole dataset (or the quarterly files) in bulk.

options.name: drug
options.about: Brand or generic name, or part of one (`Eliquis`, `apixaban`, `semaglutide`), or a Part B HCPCS code (`J9271`). Letters, digits, spaces and - / . , ( ) ' + % # &.

options.name: limit
options.about: Drugs returned per program, largest latest-year spending first.

options.name: program
options.about: Search one program; omit to search all three. `part_d`: Medicare Part D, prescriptions patients take themselves. `part_b`: Medicare Part B, drugs given in doctors' offices and hospital outpatient departments, by HCPCS code. `medicaid`: Medicaid outpatient prescriptions.

response.about: Look up what Medicare and Medicaid spend on a drug, from CMS's annual Spending by Drug datasets for Medicare Part D (prescriptions patients fill), Medicare Part B (drugs given in clinics and hospital outpatient departments, by HCPCS code) and Medicaid. Matches a brand or generic name, or part of one, case-insensitively (and a HCPCS code for Part B), and returns every matching drug per program with up to five years of total spending, dosage units, claims, beneficiaries (Medicare only), average spending per dosage unit, claim and beneficiary, CMS's outlier flag, the latest-year change and compound annual growth of unit cost, the manufacturers (Part D, Medicaid) and the Part B average sales price. Drugs come largest latest-year spending first; `datasets` gives each program's years, release date and match count. Spending is gross of manufacturer rebates. No match is an empty result.

fields.name: average_sales_price
fields.about: Part B average sales price (ASP) payment amount; null for Part D and Medicaid.

fields.name: avg_spending_per_unit_cagr
fields.about: Compound annual growth rate of average spending per dosage unit, from the first year the drug has data in the release window to the latest year; null when there is only one year of data or CMS gives none.

fields.name: avg_spending_per_unit_change
fields.about: Change in average spending per dosage unit from the year before the latest to the latest year; null when the drug has no prior-year data.

fields.name: brand_name
fields.about: As CMS writes it, without its `*` marker; generics carry the generic name here (`Atorvastatin Calcium`).

fields.name: generic_name
fields.about: Null for the Part B codes CMS lists without one.

fields.name: hcpcs_code

fields.name: hcpcs_description
fields.about: Part B HCPCS code description; null for Part D and Medicaid.

fields.name: manufacturers
fields.about: Manufacturers CMS lists for this brand and generic name, largest latest-year spending first, as CMS abbreviates them (`BMS Primarycare`). Null for Part B, which reports none.

fields.name: name_note
fields.about: What the `*` CMS appends to some names means; null when the name has none.

fields.name: program

attributes.value: This indicator is related to the national accounts, which are critical for understanding and managing a country's economy. They provide a framework for the analysis of economic performance. National accounts are the basis for estimating the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross National Income (GNI), which are the most widely used indicator of economic performance. They are essential for government policymakers, providing the data needed to design and assess fiscal and monetary policies; and are also used by businesses and investors to assess the economic climate and make investment decisions. NAS enable comparison between economies, which is crucial for international trade, investment decisions, and economic competitiveness. More specifically, this indicator is related to national accounts aggregates. Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Income (GNI), and other aggregates provide a snapshot of the size and health of an economy by measuring the total economic activity within a country. They can thus be used by policymakers to design and implement economic policies, as they reflect the overall economic performance and can indicate the need for intervention in certain areas. Aggregates also allow for comparisons between different economies, which can be useful for trade negotiations, investment decisions, and economic benchmarking. By examining aggregates over time, economists and analysts can identify trends, cycles, and potential areas of concern within an economy, and investors can use national accounts aggregates to assess the potential risks and returns of investing in a particular country. Overall, national accounts aggregates are fundamental tools for economic analysis, policy formulation, and decision-making at both the national and international levels.

Gross domestic product (GDP), though widely tracked, may not always be the most relevant summary of aggregated economic performance for all economies, especially when production occurs at the expense of consuming capital stock.









While GDP estimates based on the production approach are generally more reliable than estimates compiled from the income or expenditure side, different countries use different definitions, methods, and reporting standards. World Bank staff review the quality of national accounts data and sometimes make adjustments to improve consistency with international guidelines. Nevertheless, significant discrepancies remain between international standards and actual practice. Many statistical offices, especially those in developing countries, face severe limitations in the resources, time, training, and budgets required to produce reliable and comprehensive series of national accounts statistics.









Among the difficulties faced by compilers of national accounts is the extent of unreported economic activity in the informal or secondary economy. In developing countries a large share of agricultural output is either not exchanged (because it is consumed within the household) or not exchanged for money.

Gross domestic product is the total income earned through the production of goods and services in an economic territory during an accounting period. It can be measured in three different ways: using either the expenditure approach, the income approach, or the production approach. This indicator is expressed in current prices, meaning no adjustment has been made to account for price changes over time. This indicator is expressed in United States dollars.

Methodology: National accounts are compiled in accordance with international standards: System of National Accounts, 2008 or 1993 versions. Specific information on how countries compile their national accounts can be found on the IMF website: https://dsbb.imf.org/
Statistical concept(s): The conceptual elements of the SNA (System of National Accounts) measure what takes place in the economy, between which agents, and for what purpose. At the heart of the SNA is the production of goods and services. These may be used for consumption in the period to which the accounts relate or may be accumulated for use in a later period. In simple terms, the amount of value added generated by production represents GDP. The income corresponding to GDP is distributed to the various agents or groups of agents as income and it is the process of distributing and redistributing income that allows one agent to consume the goods and services produced by another agent or to acquire goods and services for later consumption. The way in which the SNA captures this pattern of economic flows is to identify the activities concerned by recognizing the institutional units in the economy and by specifying the structure of accounts capturing the transactions relevant to one stage or another of the process by which goods and services are produced and ultimately consumed.
Economic Policy & Debt: National accounts: US$ at current prices: Aggregate indicators

classifications.definition: An integrated continuous glucose monitoring system (iCGM) is intended to automatically measure glucose in bodily fluids continuously or frequently for a specified period of time. iCGM systems are designed to reliably and securely transmit glucose measurement data to digitally connected devices, including automated insulin dosing systems, and are intended to be used alone or in conjunction with these digitally connected medical devices for the purpose of managing a disease or condition related to glycemic control.

The device is indicated for continually measuring glucose levels in adults (age 18 and older) with diabetes for up to 90 days. The system is indicated for use to replace fingerstick blood glucose measurements for diabetes treatment decisions.The system is intended to:1)	Provide real-time glucose readings;2)	Provide glucose trend information; and3)	Provide alerts for the detection and prediction of episodes of low blood glucose (hypoglycemia) and high blood glucose (hyperglycemia).The system is a prescription device. Historical data from the system can be interpreted to aid in providing therapy adjustments. These adjustments should be based on patterns seen over time. The system is intended for single patient use.

response.text:
WARNING LETTER
WL # 724202

September 14, 2026

Dear Mr. Bonnell:

You registered your facility with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an outsourcing facility under section 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) [21 U.S.C. § 353b]1 on December 13, 2013, and most recently on December 5, 2025. From October 20, 2025, to October 30, 2025, an FDA investigator inspected your facility, SCA Pharmaceuticals, LLC located at 8821 Knoedl Court, Little Rock, Arkansas 72205. During the inspection, the investigator noted serious deficiencies in your practices for producing drug products intended or expected to be sterile, which put patients at risk.

FDA issued a Form FDA 483 to your facility on October 30, 2025. We reviewed your November 21, 2025, and December 31, 2025, responses to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Based on this inspection, it appears you produced drugs that violate the FDCA.

A. Compounded Drug Products under the FDCA

Under section 503B(b) of the FDCA, a compounder can register as an outsourcing facility with FDA. Drug products compounded by or under the direct supervision of a licensed pharmacist in an outsourcing facility qualify for exemptions from the drug approval requirements in section 505 of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 355(a)], the requirement in section 502(f)(1) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 352(f)(1)] that labeling bear adequate directions for use and the Drug Supply Chain Security Act requirements in section 582 of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 360eee-1] if the conditions in section 503B of the FDCA are met.

An outsourcing facility, which is defined in section 503B(d)(4) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 353b(d)(4)], is a facility at one geographic location or address that — (i) is engaged in the compounding of sterile drugs; (ii) has elected to register as an outsourcing facility; and (iii) complies with all of the requirements of this section. Outsourcing facilities must comply with other applicable provisions of the FDCA, including section 501(a)(2)(B) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(B)], regarding current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), and section 501(a)(2)(A) [21 U.S.C. § 351(a)(2)(A)], regarding insanitary conditions. Generally, CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products are established in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) parts 210 and 211.

B. Violations of the FDCA

Adulterated Drug Products

The FDA investigator collected evidence indicating that drug products intended or expected to be sterile were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions, whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health, causing your drug products to be adulterated under section 501(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA. For example, the investigator collected evidence indicating that:

1. Your facility lacked routine and rigorous certification of the ISO 5 areas, including airflow visualization studies performed under dynamic conditions.

2. Your firm did not perform adequate product evaluation and take appropriate corrective action after microbial contamination was recovered within the ISO 5 aseptic processing area.

3. Your component control is not adequately designed or maintained to prevent contamination of product contact surfaces due to the presence of foreign (unusual) material between the stopper ribs of syringes.

4. Your compounding technicians and aseptic assistants employ poor practices which introduce risk of microbial contamination into the ISO 5 classified critical areas during production of drugs intended to be sterile.

For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913 and/or Methadone HCl 10 mg/mL lot #1125035922, your compounding technicians:

a. Moved quickly in a critical area or in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Leaned into the hood, allowing their head and upper body to enter the ISO 5 classified critical area, thereby disrupting unidirectional airflow.

c. Blocked first pass air by placing gloved hands directly over the following:

i. Hanging IV bag ports when making sterile connections.

ii. The IV bag ports when disinfecting prior to filling.

iii. The open filled syringes and the syringe cap trays during the process of screwing caps onto the syringes.

d. Conducted aseptic operations on or directly above the hood deck surface in vertical flow hoods, which prevents unidirectional first air with minimal turbulence from surrounding aseptic operations during sterile connections and filling of drug products intended or expected to be sterile into open sterile containers.

e. Regularly rested their arms on the work surface of the hood during aseptic production. This practice may introduce contamination into the ISO 5 work area.

Additionally, your aseptic assistants:

a. Moved quickly in an area immediately adjacent to a critical area such that unidirectional airflow is likely to be disrupted.

b. Used disinfectant in a manner insufficient to achieve adequate levels of disinfection of materials, such as the IV bag ports, during transfer into the ISO 5 classified critical areas by spraying very quickly or from a significant distance or failing to treat both sides of the IV bags. Prior to disinfection, aseptic assistants regularly touched the IV bag ports in the ISO 7 area with their gloved hands.

5. Your environmental monitoring program lacks adequate routine environmental monitoring that captures data representative of aseptic production conditions. For example, during the production of Fentanyl Citrate 2 mcg/mL Bupivacaine HCl 0.125% lot #1125035913:

a. The active air sampler is placed to the far right of the hood instead of adjacent to the areas where aseptic operations occur, including the left and center portions of the ISO 5 classified hood.

b. Compounding technicians do not always carefully roll their individual fingers across the media touch plate during personnel monitoring. The compounding technician quickly touched each fingertip to the media plates instead of methodically rolling their fingertips.

6. Your firm failed to perform adequate airflow visualization studies under dynamic conditions to demonstrate unidirectional airflow within the ISO 5 area. Your airflow visualization studies are deficient because:

a. The studies do not clearly demonstrate that the airflow pattern sweeps over and away from the critical areas near and on the ISO 5 classified LAF hood work surface where aseptic operations occur. Instead, the smoke appears to arc out of the hood significantly higher than the critical area and then travel up toward the ceiling in the surrounding ISO 7 classified area.

b. In your most recent airflow visualization study VAL-25-044-FR, you indicated that (b)(4) people are allowed in ISO 7 (b)(4) Room (b)(4) during aseptic operations; however, the smoke study videos provided during the FDA inspection only include a maximum of (b)(4) people, and fail to demonstrate that airflow patterns inside the ISO 5 classified critical areas are not impacted by a large number of personnel moving inside cleanroom Room (b)(4).

The FDA investigator also collected evidence indicating CGMP violations at your facility, that caused your drug products to be adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. The violations include, for example:

1. Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures that are designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile, and that include validation of all aseptic and sterilization processes (21 CFR 211.113(b)).

2. Your firm failed to establish an adequate air supply filtered through high-efficiency particulate air filters under positive pressure in the aseptic processing areas (21 CFR 211.42(c)(10)(iii)).

3. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192).

4. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)).

5. Your firm failed to establish adequate written responsibilities and procedures applicable to the quality control unit and to follow written procedures applicable to the quality control unit (21 CFR 211.22(d)). Specifically, our review of the data collected during the inspection revealed that your firm does not maintain the production video recordings which are used to determine root causes and corrective actions during investigations. For example, after recovering microbial contamination inside the ISO 5 classified critical area during the production of Ketamine HCl 10 mg/mL lot 1125035065, your Quality Unit evaluated the production video recording as part of excursion investigation EXC-2025-0045 to examine aseptic practices for potential root causes. However, instead of retaining the video recording as a quality related document, you only retained still images. Your Chief Quality Officer stated that video recordings are kept for approximately (b)(4) before being overwritten.

Outsourcing facilities must comply with CGMP requirements under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FDCA. FDA’s regulations regarding CGMP requirements for the preparation of drug products have been established in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211. FDA intends to promulgate more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities. FDA has issued a revised draft guidance, Current Good Manufacturing Practice — Guidance for Human Drug Compounding Outsourcing Facilities under Section 503B of the FD&C Act. This draft guidance, when finalized, will describe FDA’s expectations regarding outsourcing facilities and the CGMP requirements in 21 CFR parts 210 and 211 until more specific CGMP regulations for outsourcing facilities are promulgated.

Under section 301(a) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(a)], the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce of any drug that is adulterated is a prohibited act. Further, it is also a prohibited act under section 301(k) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(k)] to do any act with respect to a drug, if such act is done while the drug is held for sale after shipment in interstate commerce and results in the drug being adulterated.

C. Corrective Actions

We have reviewed your facility’s responses to the Form FDA 483 dated November 21, 2025, and December 31, 2025.

Some of your corrective actions appear adequate. However, we are unable to fully evaluate some of your corrective actions due to lack of adequate supporting documentation:

1. Although you stated that you performed airflow visualization studies in all (b)(4) hoods, you did not clearly demonstrate that these studies were performed in all (b)(4) hoods during the most recent airflow visualization assessment, performed in 2025. Additionally, while you concluded that the hoods are identical and therefore functionally equivalent, this approach does not account for potential variations in the HEPA filter performance, for example, resulting from particulate accumulation over time, nor the impact of physical placement of hoods within the room—including proximity to doors, return vents, and other environmental factors that may affect airflow where production activities are occurring.

Some of your corrective actions appear deficient:

1. You did not demonstrate that the probable root cause of inadequate material sanitization had no impact on the released portions of the batch associated with microbial excursions in the ISO 5 classified areas during production. You indicated both in your investigations and in your response that your material sanitization process is robust, but also concluded that the microbial contamination was most likely due to inadequate material sanitization.

You failed to demonstrate that microbial contamination was not present in the materials associated with the released portions of the batch. You did not demonstrate that the material sanitization process for the released portions of the batches did not include the same deficiencies as the material sanitization for the rejected portion of the batch. Further, you failed to initiate any corrective and preventative action plans to determine whether you need to improve your material sanitization process to prevent reoccurrence.

2. It appears that your visual inspection system is inadequate because you classify particulate defects as major and therefore only characterize and investigate the observed particles when the defect rate is above the major defect threshold of (b)(4)%. Extrinsic particulates should be classified as critical, and the intrinsic particulates should be evaluated based on multiple factors, including particle size and route of administration, to determine the appropriate defect classification. Your SOP ILP-001-LR, Product Inspection and Defect Classification, states, “If a DRL (Defect Rate Limit) threshold is exceeded related to ‘Particulate/material in solution,’ the particulate/material must be identified during the event.” According to your visual inspection data, you detected between (b)(4) and (b)(4) particles in (b)(4) separate lots between April 2025 and September 2025, only (b)(4) lots of which exceeded the (b)(4)% threshold for major defects. According to your Deviation log, only (b)(4) defect incidents were investigated between April 2025 and September 2025, and these were related to any Defect Rate Limit Threshold Exceedance, not just those involving particles. Therefore, you do not have an adequate system in place to ensure that you identify and appropriately investigate contaminating particles.

3. You did not commit to revising the minor defect classification for “[f]oreign (unusual) material, e.g., cardboard trapped between stopper ribs” to account for the criticality of the foreign material. While you noted that any units exhibiting this defect are rejected, the defect rate limit applied to minor defects ((b)(4)%) is not appropriate for adequately investigating, trending, and performing corrective actions, as necessary, to mitigate this contamination risk.

You did not provide adequate documentation to demonstrate that foreign materials are contained within the ribs of the syringe stoppers in non-product-contact area and will not pose contamination risks to the drug product. In addition, the syringe filling process demonstrates that the foreign material does come into contact with product-contact area of the syringes. For example, any cardboard particles trapped within the syringe ribs may be pressed against the inner syringe wall during filling, potentially introducing particles onto a surface that subsequently contacts the drug product solution.

In addition to the issues discussed above, you should note that CGMP requires the implementation of quality oversight and controls over the manufacture of drugs, including the safety of raw materials, materials used in drug manufacturing, and finished drug products. See section 501 of the FDCA. If you choose to contract with a laboratory to perform some functions required by CGMP, it is essential that you select a qualified contractor and that you maintain sufficient oversight of the contractor’s operations to ensure that it is fully CGMP compliant. Regardless of whether you rely on a contract facility, you are responsible for assuring that drugs you produce are neither adulterated nor misbranded. [See 21 CFR 210.1(b), 21 CFR 200.10(b).]

FDA strongly recommends that your management undertake a comprehensive assessment of operations, including facility design, procedures, personnel, processes, maintenance, materials, and systems. In particular, this review should assess your aseptic processing operations. A third-party consultant with relevant sterile drug manufacturing expertise should assist you in conducting this comprehensive evaluation.

D. Conclusion

The violations cited in this letter are not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations at your facility. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations.

You should take prompt action to address any violations. Failure to adequately address any violations may result in legal action without further notice, including, without limitation, seizure and injunction.

Within fifteen (15) working days of receipt of this letter, please notify this office in writing of the specific steps that you have taken to address any violations. Please include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. If you believe your products are not in violation of the FDCA, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. If you cannot completely address this matter within fifteen (15) working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so.

All correspondence should refer to the Warning Letter Number above (# 724202) and include a subject line that clearly identifies the submission as a Response to Warning Letter. If you have questions regarding the contents of this letter, please contact compoundinginspections@fda.hhs.gov.

Sincerely,
/S/

Matthew J. Lash
Acting Director
Office of Compounding Quality and Compliance
Office of Compliance
Center for Drug Evaluation and Research

cc: Scott P. Luce, Chief Executive Officer

response.text:
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955.

The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program
The Fed's Discount Window: 1990 to the Present

response.location: At the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
response.speaker: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
response.text:
Thank you for the opportunity to speak at the Treasury Market Conference. Today I will discuss modernization of the Federal Reserve's discount window and some implications of that modernization for Treasury market functioning.1

As this group knows well, the Federal Reserve's discount window lending program provides liquidity to banks.2 Banks access discount window liquidity overwhelmingly through primary credit borrowing, which is offered on a "no questions asked" basis. The discount window is as old as the Federal Reserve itself, which will be 113 years old in December.3 Over its long history, the Federal Reserve has used the discount window to support the liquidity and stability of the banking system and to implement monetary policy. For the discount window to continue to do so, it is important that the discount window evolves with the banking and financial system. That is why the staff at the Board of Governors and at each Federal Reserve Bank have worked diligently over the past several years to enhance discount window operations. The continuing efforts to modernize the discount window ensure a more efficient, accessible source of liquidity that banks can access quickly and without hesitation when needed.

Of course, the Treasury market arguably is as old as our country itself, with the origins of federal debt dating back to the Revolutionary War.4 That said, the beginnings of the modern Treasury market are more directly traced to World War I.5 Over the past century, the Treasury market has evolved into one of the deepest and most liquid markets in the world.

In the Federal Reserve System, there is an array of responsibilities among Reserve Banks and the Board regarding the discount window. The Reserve Banks operate the discount window in their Districts, and the Board provides oversight and establishes policy through regulations and guidance to Reserve Banks. Because policy and operations are closely intertwined, the Board coordinates extensively with Reserve Bank leadership and staff on discount window matters. I have the privilege of serving as the Oversight Governor for the Division of Monetary Affairs. In that capacity, I oversee the Board's work on discount window policy.

Today I will discuss the progress we have made in recent years to further modernize the discount window. Then, I will speak briefly about the role of Treasury securities as collateral for discount window loans. But, first, I cannot overemphasize that modernizing discount window operations is a true Systemwide effort and that teamwork is key. While notable strides have been made, there is still important work to do. I look forward to seeing continued improvements in discount window operations in the coming years.

Three Dimensions of Discount Window Modernization Now, I will move on to what we are doing at the Federal Reserve to modernize the discount window to meet 21st-century banking needs.6 Over the past few years, the System has conducted extensive outreach to banks and other stakeholders to understand better their experiences with the discount window, including the Board's issuance of a request for information (RFI) on discount window operations in 2024. This RFI complemented the ongoing conversations with the public that occur at all levels and in multiple corners of the Federal Reserve System, such as Ask the Fed® sessions and Reserve Bank outreach events. We have made progress in addressing feedback received through these various channels as part of our modernization efforts and are implementing improvements so banks can benefit as quickly as possible.

I think of the System's work on discount window modernization along three dimensions: business process improvements, automation enhancements, and coordination with the Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLBs).

First, ongoing business process improvements have been supporting better efficiency and standardization. Reserve Banks have focused on providing banks with more efficient access to the discount window. In terms of standardization, all Districts work within the same collateral framework, use common loan valuation models and processing technology, and accept electronic signatures. Earlier this month, the Reserve Banks took an important step to further simplify and streamline how banks pledge loans as collateral.7 These changes allow eligible institutions to pledge several different loan types to maximize liquidity while maintaining possession of the collateral. The recently enacted changes include simplified forms, faster enrollment, automated pledged loan lists, and centralized resources so that institutions can easily find the information they need. These process improvements further enhance consistency in collateral administration across the 12 Reserve Banks while still maintaining robust risk-management practices.

Second, we have enhanced the discount window user experience. In 2024, the System launched Discount Window Direct (DWD), a self-service online portal that allows banks to request loans, make payments, view loan and collateral information, and submit loan collateral files electronically. Since the portal's launch, users have reported that it is now faster, easier, and more efficient to borrow from the discount window. Today, over 60 percent of discount window loan requests are submitted through DWD. The portal also includes a messaging feature that allows banks to directly message their local Reserve Bank in lieu of a phone call. Faster, more efficient discount window access gives banks greater certainty as they manage fast-moving liquidity needs. As adoption grows and new features are added, this technology will continue improving the discount window experience.

Third, and very important, is our collaboration with the FHLBs. As many of you may know, the FHLBs are important liquidity providers to banking organizations, and both the Federal Reserve and FHLB Systems share the goal of supporting the stability and resilience of the U.S. banking system. Given the increased speed with which liquidity can now move, a key focus of ours has been reducing the time it takes to re-allocate collateral by enhancing interoperability between Reserve Banks and FHLBs.

Efforts to date have focused on improving preparedness through measures that support coordination and collaboration between Reserve Banks and FHLBs—this initiative includes reinforcing relationships, establishing back-end operational arrangements and documentation, and developing processes that enable Reserve Banks and FHLBs to work together more effectively. We and our FHLB partners believe our ongoing efforts and continued commitment to this coordination put us in a much better position than three years ago by meaningfully improving our processes and strengthening relationships and engagement between the two Systems.

On a personal note, I have had an opportunity to engage with the FHLB presidents and other leaders in the FHLB System, and I appreciate greatly their ongoing collaboration and support as we continue to work together on interoperability. This engagement is not just about crisis preparedness—it is also about building lasting, more effective institutional partnerships.

Of course, the Federal Reserve's work on enhancements to the discount window is a continuous process. In over a century, the discount window has evolved from a physical teller window at a Reserve Bank that a bank representative had to visit to an online portal that permits a bank to request a loan with a few clicks. We are living through an era of rapid economic and technological transformation, and it will be crucial that the discount window continues to evolve and respond to our ever-changing environment. The modernization efforts I have described make discount window borrowing faster and less operationally burdensome. These improvements, I believe, help reduce the frictions that may make banks hesitant to use the window when they are healthy and reinforce overall confidence in the banking system. Our work is not done, but I remain committed to working with my colleagues throughout the Federal Reserve System to do just that.

Treasury Securities as Discount Window Collateral This commitment brings me to an increasingly important dimension of discount window operations. A well-functioning Treasury market is essential to the stability and the efficiency of the financial system and the economy more broadly. The U.S. Treasury market serves as the foundation for pricing risk across all asset classes, facilitating the efficient allocation of capital throughout our economy. In this context, the discount window supports Treasury market resilience in important ways. By providing banks with a reliable source of liquidity, the discount window serves as a shock absorber during periods of market stress by reducing the risk of forced sales of Treasury securities. Moreover, the discount window's stabilizing influence extends to broader money markets. By alleviating funding pressures at depository institutions, the discount window helps ensure the smooth functioning of key short-term funding markets—including the repurchase agreement (repo) market and the federal funds market. This dynamic, in turn, supports Treasury market liquidity.

Institutions holding Treasury securities in their Fedwire Securities accounts can quickly transfer them to their discount window pledge account even late in the day. For institutions that have arrangements in place, this means that pledging Treasury collateral and receiving a same-day loan are straightforward and efficient. This speed and ease of access matter for market functioning, particularly when banks active in the Treasury market need liquidity quickly. The COVID-19 crisis demonstrated this predicament clearly. In March 2020, when the Treasury market experienced severe dysfunction, we saw a sharp increase in Treasury securities pledged to the Federal Reserve to secure potential discount window loans. The Federal Reserve's ability to accept Treasury securities quickly and to provide banks with the option of obtaining reserves if they were needed proved critical.8

The discount window also helps respond to sudden tightening in money markets, supporting the Federal Reserve's monetary policy implementation and complementing the standing repo operations in relieving funding market pressures. When pressures emerge in money markets, banks can turn to the discount window rather than borrowing at rates above the Federal Reserve's target range. Indeed, we have recently seen more use of the discount window amid periods associated with temporary upward pressure on money market rates, such as those observed at quarter-ends.

The interaction between the Treasury market and the discount window that I have described underscores why maintaining a robust and effective discount window framework is not merely about banks, but critically important for financial stability more broadly.

Conclusion As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, the Federal Reserve's ability to lend to banks through the discount window dates to the System's founding and is one of our core functions. This liquidity provision serves a variety of purposes: it facilitates the ability of banks to lend to households and businesses and supports other financial market participants during stress or volatile market conditions. It is particularly important for Treasury markets that banks can serve as a source of strength for market functioning. The discount window's acceptance of Treasury securities as collateral with same-day value helps make this stability possible.

Today the discount window remains ready to lend smoothly and effectively to banks when needed. The modernization efforts I have discussed will ensure that the discount window supports individual banking institutions and broader market resilience well into the future. To be sure, we cannot be complacent when it comes to the discount window. Ultimately, I believe that the continued success of the discount window, as with many endeavors, lies with the ongoing partnership and dedication of various stakeholders within the Federal Reserve System and those external to it, including many of you here today. Working together, we will continue to fulfill the fundamental purpose of the discount window as established over a century ago—and thereby achieve the best outcomes for the American people.

Thank you.

1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text

2. See Philip N. Jefferson (2024), "A History of the Fed's Discount Window: 1913–2000," speech delivered at Davidson College, Davidson, N.C., October 8. Return to text

3. See Federal Reserve Act, Pub. L. No. 63-43, 38 Stat. 251 (December 23, 1913). Return to text

4. See Richard Sylla and David J. Cowen (2018), Alexander Hamilton on Finance, Credit, and Debt (New York: Columbia University Press). Return to text

5. See Kenneth D. Garbade (2012), Birth of a Market: The U.S. Treasury Securities Market from the Great War to the Great Depression (Cambridge: MIT Press). Return to text

6. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "Discount Window Modernization," webpage. Return to text

7. See Federal Reserve Discount Window (2026), "The Federal Reserve Implements Improvements and Streamlines the Borrower-in-Custody Program," webpage, September 8. Return to text

8. For a discussion of the discount window's role in recent stress episodes, see Philip N. Jefferson (2024) "The Fed's Discount Window: 1990 to the Present," speech delivered at the Charlotte Economics Club, Charlotte, N.C., October 9. Return to text

datasets.notes_and_known_limitations:
***Total Public Debt Outstanding Disclaimer***

There are six datasets on Fiscal Data which include the national debt, which is referred to as Total Public Debt Outstanding (TPDO). TPDO is the sum of Debt Held by the Public and Intragovernmental (Intragov) Holdings. Some datasets include debt issued by the Federal Financing Bank (FFB). The datasets listed below only include debt issued by the Treasury Department. The list below provides information on where there are differences in debt calculations related to the national debt.

Debt to the Penny contains TPDO, as well as a breakout of Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings. In this dataset, Intragov Holdings includes debt issued by the FFB.

Historical Debt Outstanding contains TPDO, but no breakout of Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings. In this dataset, TPDO includes debt issued by the FFB.

Daily Treasury Statement (DTS) contains Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings, but does not aggregate these two categories into TPDO. In this dataset, Intragov Holdings includes debt issued by the FFB. Dollar values for Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings are rounded in millions to cohere with other data in the dataset. Please note that the published reports on the Fiscal Service site contain TPDO values.

Monthly Treasury Statement (MTS) contains TPDO, as well as a breakout of Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings. In this dataset, Intragov Holdings includes debt issued by the FFB.

Monthly Statement of the Public Debt (MSPD) contains TPDO, as well as a breakout of Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings. In this dataset, Intragov Holdings includes debt issued by the FFB. Dollar values are rounded in millions to cohere with other data in the dataset.

Schedules of Federal Debt contains Debt Held by the Public and Intragov Holdings, but does not aggregate these two categories into TPDO. In this dataset, Intragov Holdings do not include debt issued by the FFB. Dollar values are rounded in millions to cohere with other data in the dataset.

***End Total Public Debt Outstanding Disclaimer***

Debt broken out by intragovernmental holdings and debt held by the public has not always been provided. Where this occurred, the dataset shows a value of $0.00 instead of a null value. Debt held by the public and intragovernmental holdings data is available yearly (on a fiscal basis) from 9/30/1997 through 9/30/2001, monthly from 9/30/2001 through 3/31/2005, and daily from 4/4/2005 to today. Some columns in this dataset overlap with the [Monthly Statement of the Public Debt (MSPD)](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/monthly-statement-public-debt/), [Monthly Treasury Statement (MTS)](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/monthly-treasury-statement/), [Daily Treasury Statement (DTS)](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/daily-treasury-statement/), and [Schedules of Federal Debt](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/schedules-federal-debt/) datasets. Debt issued by the Federal Financing Bank (FFB) is included in the intragovernmental holdings in the Debt to the Penny dataset, but not in the Schedules of Federal Debt dataset because it is not debt managed by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service. The difference between these datasets is equal to the amount of debt issued by the FFB.

Downloaded CSV files with values greater than $10 trillion may have the final two digits (cents) excluded due to digit limits enforced by the application used to access the file. The JSON and XML file downloads are not impacted by this limitation.

Total Public Debt Outstanding = Debt Held by the Public + Intragovernmental Holdings

Please note that Total Public Debt Outstanding may be calculated differently within different datasets. See those datasets Notes & Known Limitations section for calculation details.
